\paragraph{CSD dissociation and the cascade mechanism.}
Classical critical slowing down (CSD) analysis reveals a striking dissociation between canary and downstream metrics.
Canary metrics (token entropy, ECE) exhibit clear CSD signatures: Kendall $\tau{=}0.79$--$0.82$ for AR(1) trend and $\tau{=}0.73$--$0.88$ for variance trend ($p{<}0.001$ in all cases).
Downstream diversity metrics (distinct-1/2/3) show no CSD ($\tau{=}0.03$--$0.30$, $p{>}0.19$).
This dissociation suggests a \emph{canary-triggered cascade}: canary metrics gradually destabilize (second-order CSD) while downstream metrics undergo abrupt transitions (first-order) without prior warning signals in their own time series.
Combined with the four-layer taxonomy, this yields a four-stage cascade ordered by contamination threshold:
(1)~structural change ($\alpha{\geq}0.10$: effective rank contracts);
(2)~canary destabilization ($\alpha{\geq}0.25$: CSD present in entropy/ECE, $10\times$ variance inflation);
(3)~causal lead-lag emergence ($\alpha{\geq}0.50$: PermG crosses power threshold);
(4)~full cascade ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$: multi-seed, multi-method detection).
Within the blind zone ($\alpha{<}0.50$), canary CSD is present but no lead-lag is detectable---the system is destabilizing without yet producing a temporal offset that Granger tests can capture.
Token entropy AC1 exhibits a $+0.30$ jump at the onset boundary (from $-0.58$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ to $-0.28$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$); although AC1 remains negative throughout, the direction aligns with the CSD prediction that autocorrelation increases near critical transitions~\cite{scheffer2009early}.
The anomalously negative AC1 at $\alpha{=}0.45$ ($-0.58$) may reflect critical speeding-up~\cite{titus2020speeding}, where indicators exhibit non-monotonic behavior immediately before a transition.
These CSD patterns are suggestive but not statistically conclusive at $T{=}11$, where the 95\% confidence interval for AC1 is approximately $\pm 0.3$; longer generation protocols ($T{\geq}50$--$100$) would be needed for formal CSD testing~\cite{dakos2012methods}.

\paragraph{Suggestive CSD signatures.}
Exploratory analysis reveals a CSD-consistent pattern: canary metrics show rising autocorrelation (Kendall $\tau{=}0.79$--$0.82$, $p{<}0.001$) while downstream diversity metrics show none ($\tau{=}0.03$--$0.30$, $p{>}0.19$), suggestive of a temporal sequence in which canary destabilization precedes downstream collapse.
However, this dissociation does not survive multiple testing correction (2/10 conditions significant post-BH), and surrogate-based validation would be needed to confirm CSD against colored-noise alternatives~\cite{dakos2012methods}.

Raw metric drift from generation~0 to generation~10 is summarized in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary}.


\subsection{Detection Phase Transition}
\label{sec:regime}

Diversity collapse occurs at every contamination level: distinct-1 declines by $14.1\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (fine-tuning drift) and by $40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (3-seed mean).
Despite this ubiquitous degradation, causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent.
Permutation Granger (PermG) tests find 0/8 canary$\to$downstream pairs FDR-significant from $\alpha{=}0.00$ through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jump to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (2~fp32 seeds, consistent).
This transition is striking because cumulative synthetic fraction barely changes across the boundary: $C = 1{-}(1{-}\alpha)^{10}$ yields $99.75\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ versus $99.90\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a difference of 0.15 percentage points, yet detection jumps from null to reliable.

\label{sec:intervention}

We implement a predictive cessation protocol: training with synthetic data ($\alpha{=}1.0$) continues until token entropy drops ${>}15\%$ relative to generation~0, at which point $\alpha$ switches to $0.0$ (pure real data).

\subsection{Cross-Architecture Generalization}
\label{sec:generalization}

We evaluate the detection phase transition across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (Pythia, GPT-2, OPT, Qwen, SmolLM3, Padding-variant), scales from 345M to 6.9B parameters, and two training domains (WikiText-103, C4).
Table~\ref{tab:generalization} reports PermG forward detection at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
PermG forward significance reaches ${\geq}$6/8 in 13 of 15 conditions (87\%).
Two exceptions emerge: Pythia-1.4B seed~42 on WikiText (2/8), a seed-dependent outlier that recovers to 6/8 in seed~43, and SmolLM3-3B (3/8), where only ECE$\to$downstream pairs reach significance while entropy$\to$downstream pairs fail entirely (0/4; details in Appendix).
SmolLM3's token entropy exhibits non-monotonic oscillations across generations; this pattern violates the monotonic decline that Granger tests require.
The onset boundary $\alpha_c \approx 0.50$ at $T{=}10$ is architecture-independent: every family that achieves detection does so at or above this threshold, and none achieves reliable detection below it.

Replacing WikiText-103 with C4 yields the strongest detection observed: Pythia-1B reaches PermG~fwd 8/8 (2~seeds), and Pythia-1.4B reaches 8/8 on C4 versus 2/8 on WikiText at the same scale.
At Pythia-6.9B (bf16), detection recovers to 7/8 on WikiText.
Dataset characteristics modulate detection power independently of model capacity.
Directional asymmetry also varies by domain: at $\alpha{=}0.50$ on C4, PermG reverse reaches 7/8, compared to 0/24 across all WikiText conditions.
This domain-dependent bidirectionality suggests that the unidirectional forward causation observed on WikiText may partly reflect domain-specific dynamics (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\subsection{Canary-Based Early Intervention}
\label{sec:intervention}

We implement a predictive cessation protocol: training with synthetic data ($\alpha{=}1.0$) continues until token entropy drops ${>}15\%$ relative to generation~0, at which point $\alpha$ switches to $0.0$ (pure real data).
A reactive baseline triggers when distinct-1 drops ${>}10\%$.
The predictive trigger fires at generation~1 in both Pythia-410M and Pythia-1.4B (s42 fp32), one generation before the reactive baseline (generation~2).
Peak perplexity under predictive intervention is $56.99$ versus $157.09$ under reactive (s42 fp32), a 58\% reduction (bootstrap 95\% CI: 29--64\%).
Recovery occurs at generation~2 under predictive cessation versus generation~4 under reactive.
Both models converge to the $\alpha{=}0.0$ baseline by generation~10.

The trigger generation, recovery timeline, and convergence behavior are identical across the $3.4\times$ scale gap from 410M to 1.4B, and the 15\% entropy threshold generalizes without recalibration.
These results position canary-based detection within a four-layer taxonomy of collapse monitoring: (1)~dimensionality collapse, detectable at $\alpha \geq 0.10$ via $n$-gram diversity decline; (2)~distributional variance, detectable at $\alpha \geq 0.25$ via calibration drift; (3)~causal coupling, detectable at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ via Granger precedence; and (4)~dynamical stability, assessable at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ via lag structure.
Each layer captures a distinct aspect of collapse, and lower layers activate at lower contamination thresholds.
The practical implication is that canary monitoring should combine multiple detection layers rather than rely on any single statistical test.
